abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered promising candidate materials for next‐generation nuclear reactors due to their superior mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability at high temperatures. However, the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu, commonly used in cooling systems, poses challenges in forming composite structures. This study addresses the issue using a liquid metal dealloying (LMD) process. A precursor alloy (WTaVTi) with a directional dendrite‐interdendrite structure is fabricated and reacted with molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h. This approach produced a RHEA‐Cu composite with a stable interface between RHEA (W31.5Ta30.9V21.4Ti14.3) and Cu, featuring a spontaneously formed W‐rich interlayer that enhances interfacial bonding. The composite showed excellent irradiation resistance, with 30% less swelling under α‐ion irradiation than pure W. It also exhibited low thermal conductivity at room temperature, but reached ≈120 W m−1·K−1 at ≈650 °C, surpassing pure W. This temperature‐dependent rise in κ, with a positive gradient of +0.075 W m−1·K− 2, is attributed to decreasing diffuse mismatch at elevated temperatures. The large‐scale reaction and stable microstructure achieved through LMD process highlight its industrial potential. This work offers a strategy for developing high‐performance materials by combining RHEA's radiation resistance with Cu's thermal conductivity for extreme environments.

This study focuses on developing a composite of the refractory high entropy alloy WTaVTi with Cu, using a liquid metal dealloying process. The resulting composite features highly thermally conductive Cu channels embedded between ligaments of RHEA, which exhibits excellent irradiation resistance. The synergy between these materials introduces a novel approach to producing nuclear materials designed for extreme environments.

sec.title: Introduction

caption.p: Schematic diagrams of various existing methods for fabricating W‐Cu composites: a) Cu melt infiltration into a W skeleton, b) spark plasma sintering of W and Cu powders, c) mechanical alloying, and (d) 3D printing.

sec.p: In this study, WTaVTi RHEA, characterized by a microstructure of W‐rich dendrites and Ti‐rich interdendritic (ID) regions, was used as the precursor in the LMD process. Preferential reactions were induced in the ID regions within a pure Cu melt, ensuring robust thermal conductivity (κ) in the Cu‐rich phase formed by the process. This approach facilitated faster and more uniform reactions, maximizing the synergistic properties of each phase. The resulting RHEA‐Cu composite exhibited superior κ compared to pure W at temperatures exceeding ≈650 °C. Moreover, this composite retains the inherent HEA characteristic of increasing κ with an increase of temperature, thereby serving as an even more effective heat transfer material at elevated temperatures. Consequently, owing to this attribute, the composite holds significant promise for high‐temperature applications—such as in nuclear reactor environments—where it not only provides the enhanced mechanical properties and irradiation resistance afforded by its composite structure, but also delivers superior thermal conductivity. To further investigate the mechanisms underlying these remarkable properties, detailed microstructural and phase characterizations of each phase were conducted using TEM analysis. The RHEA‐Cu composite developed in this study holds significant promise for diverse applications, not only as a foundational material for next‐generation nuclear reactors and fusion power plants but also for thermal dissipation in extreme operational environments.

sec.title: Alloy Design of WTaVTi Precursor for the LMD Process
sec.p:
Figure
2a depicts the thermodynamic relationships between the elements in the WTaVTi RHEA and the Cu. This figure highlights why Ti is the most suitable sacrificial element for the LMD reaction employed in this study. An ideal sacrificial element for the LMD process should satisfy the following criteria: 1) it should readily form a solid solution with other alloying elements in the precursor alloy without forming any secondary phases. 2) it should exhibit a negative ΔHmix with the liquid metal (Cu), and 3) it should possess a relatively low melting point to enable rapid diffusion in the molten metal bath. Ti meets all of these requirements. Specifically, Ti is known to form a disordered BCC (A2) solid solution with W, Ta, and V, ensuring stable precursor alloy formation. At the same time, it exhibits a negative ΔHmix of –9 kJ mol−1 with Cu, in stark contrast to the other RHEA constituents—W, Ta, and V—which exhibit positive ΔHmix values of +22, +2, and +5 kJ mol−1, respectively.[
8
] Furthermore, Ti has the lowest melting point (1668 °C) among Group 4 elements, enabling faster diffusion in the melt. Consequently, Ti is preferentially selected as the sacrificial element that undergoes atomic exchange with Cu and is subsequently removed from the precursor, while Group 5 and 6 transition metals, including W, remain in the HEA phase due to their immiscibility with Cu.

caption.p: Thermodynamic design of the precursor alloy for the LMD process. a) Thermodynamic relationships between the Cu melt involved in the LMD process and the alloying elements with positive and negative ΔHmix with Cu. b) Pseudo‐binary phase diagram of the precursor material, WTaVTi alloy. The diagram is constructed with WTaV, which exhibits positive ΔHmix with Cu, as one axis based on thermodynamic considerations. c) Microstructure of the precursor with D‐ID structure and its EDS results.

sec.p: Figure 2b presents the pseudo‐binary phase diagram of the WTaVTi alloy tailored for the LMD process. Using Ti as the sacrificial component on one axis and assuming complete solid solution formation for WTaV on the other, the diagram predicts a uniform BCC solid solution phase at temperatures above 1200 K (≈930 °C). The liquidus temperature of the WTaV phase, which constitutes the ligaments in the RHEA‐Cu composite, is ≈3110 K, indicating the possibility of having excellent high‐temperature mechanical properties. Based on this phase diagram, a precursor alloy with an equiatomic composition of all four elements was selected. This composition includes ≈25 at.% Ti, which is expected to yield a composite with an estimated 30 vol% of Cu‐rich phase, if all of the Ti atoms had position exchange with Cu.

Besides, formation of the ordered B2 phase is also predicted in compositions containing 15–75 at.% Ti at temperatures below 1150 K (≈0.48Tm). Nevertheless, the formation of this phase is unlikely due to the rapid quenching employed during the precursor casting process using water‐cooled Cu molds. Furthermore, in Ti‐rich compositions with more than 85 at.% Ti, the formation of the disordered HCP (A3) phase is expected in similar temperature ranges (indicated in the blue region of the diagram). However, in the equiatomic precursor composition utilized in this study, which contains over 25 at.% Ti, the formation of the HCP phase during conventional alloy casting is improbable.

Figure 2c illustrates the microstructure of the as‐cast precursor material, emphasizing the RHEA dendrites that will form the ligament regions in the composite. The lower panel of the figure presents the compositional distribution of the dendritic‐interdendritic (D‐ID) structure, analyzed using EDS. According to the EDS line scan, the dendrites are enriched with high‐melting‐point elements W and Ta, exhibiting a composition of W37.5Ta28.9V17.8Ti15.8. In contrast, the ID regions are enriched with low‐melting‐point elements Ti and V, with a composition of W9.9Ta17.7V35.8Ti36.6. Detailed data provided in Table
1 indicate a D‐ID phase volume ratio of ≈7:3. This segregation occurs because, during solidification, the high‐melting‐point elements W and Ta preferentially form dendrites, while the low‐melting‐point elements Ti and V are redistributed into the liquid phase, forming the ID regions.

caption.p: Compositional constituent of as‐cast precursor, and RHEA‐Cu composite fabricated by LMD process.

sec.title: WTaVTi Precursor's Mechanical Property and Irradiation Resistance
sec.p:
RHEAs are renowned for their exceptional mechanical properties at both ambient and elevated temperatures.[
21 , 22
] These attributes, particularly their high‐temperature strength and phase stability, are critical for their application in nuclear materials. To predict the mechanical properties of the final composite produced via the LMD process, the compressive stress‐strain curves of as‐cast RHEAs, including the WTaVTi precursor alloy, were measured, as shown in Figure
3a. To investigate the effect of alloying elements on mechanical properties, stress‐strain curves were analyzed for a series of as‐cast RHEAs, beginning with unary pure W and sequentially adding elements to form binary (WTa), ternary (WTaV), and quaternary (WTaVTi, the precursor) systems.

caption.p: As‐cast WTaVTi alloy with excellent mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. a) Compressive stress‐strain curves of four alloys: W, WTa, WTaV, and WTaVTi. b) He‐induced volumetric swelling of each alloy as a function of He concentration under α‐ion (He+) irradiation. (b‐2) AFM image showing surface blister cracking caused by alpha‐ion irradiation.

sec.p:
At this point, the two most representative methods for estimating the strength of a composite are as follows. Under Voigt's assumption of isostrain, where the entire material deforms uniformly under the same strain, the composite strength can be expressed as: σ = σ m
Vm + σ f
Vf . In contrast, under Reuss's assumption of isostress, where the material experiences uniform stress but different strains, the composite strength is given by: 1σ=Vmσm+Vfσf. In practical cases, the YS of the composite generally falls between the predictions of Voigt's and Reuss's assumptions. The YS, defined as the stress at the end of the elastic region, can thus be approximated using these equations.

In this study, 25 keV α‐ions were implanted into the materials, and He induced swelling was analyzed using AFM. Figure 3b shows the swelling height of each material as a function of the average implanted He concentration. All alloys displayed increasing swelling height with the increase of the He concentration. (The dpa and He concentrations, which vary with the irradiation depth for each alloy, were calculated using SRIM simulation. The detailed results are presented in Figure S3, Supporting Information). For pure W and the WTaVTi precursor alloy, blistering was observed under sustained irradiation. Up to ≈27 at.% of He implantation (fluence ≈4 × 10¹⁷ atoms cm− 2, ≈15 dpa), all alloys experience similar behavior under this condition.

As the number of implanted ions increases, defect clustering leads to blistering, which eventually results in surface cracking. This cracking mechanism releases strain energy, halting further swelling. To validate this mechanism, α‐ion implantation was conducted on pure W and the WTaVTi RHEA until cracks formed, as shown in Figure 3(b‐2). As shown in this figure, most of the observed swelling is understood to result from the formation of helium bubbles. Both materials showed sharp increases in swelling height beyond a fluence of 4 × 10¹⁷ atoms cm− 2 (≈14 at.% of He concentration), with cracks appearing at 8 × 10¹⁷ atoms cm− 2 for W and 8.5 × 10¹⁷ atoms cm− 2 (≈60 at.% of He concentration)for WTaVTi. The swelling heights at these fluences were 137% for W and 108% for WTaVTi. Notably, the RHEA exhibited ≈30% lower swelling and resisted blistering until a fluence ≈4 × 10¹⁷ atoms cm− 2 higher than pure W. These findings underscore the potential of the WTaVTi alloy as an advanced material for nuclear and fusion cooling systems, combining reduced swelling and greater resistance to blistering‐induced failure.

sec.title: Fabrication of RHEA‐Cu Composite via LMD Process
sec.p:
A unique RHEA‐Cu composite was successfully fabricated by reacting the WTaVTi RHEA in a Cu melt bath. Figure
4a,b illustrate the WTaVTi precursor alloy and the resulting composite microstructure obtained through the reaction. As shown in Figure 2 and Table 1, the precursor alloy exhibited a D‐ID structure in the as‐cast state, with the ID region containing ≈36.6% Ti, which is prone to dissolve into Cu. The average dendritic first‐arm thickness was ≈11.3 µm (±1.42), accounting for ≈71% of the total volume fraction, while the Ti‐rich ID regions displayed spacings of 2–5 µm depending on location. The XRD trace (brown) in Figure 4c confirmed that the as‐cast RHEA consisted of a single BCC phase. With this single‐phase precursor alloy, the RHEA precursor and Cu melt were sealed in a silica tube under vacuum. The precursor, shaped as a 1‐mm‐thick, 4‐mm‐diameter coin to comply with LFA ASTM standards, was reacted at 1200 °C for 96 h. According to the phase diagram in Figure 2b, this temperature ensured the RHEA maintained a complete solid solution without phase separation or precipitate formation, facilitating a homogeneous reaction.

caption.p: Microstructures before and after the LMD process. a) Microstructure of the as‐cast WTaVTi precursor prior to the LMD process. b) Microstructure of the composite formed after reacting with a Cu melt at 1200 °C for 96 h, showing the complete substitution of the ID region in Figure 4a with Cu. c) XRD traces before and after the LMD reaction, along with EDS maps illustrating the elemental distribution post‐reaction: d) Cu, e) W, f) Ta, g) V, and h) Ti.

sec.p: The resulting composite microstructure, shown in Figure 4b, retained bright and dark contrasts, indicating the formation of distinct regions due to the interaction between Cu and Ti in the ID regions. The XRD results (red trace) in Figure 4c confirmed a composite structure comprising BCC RHEA ligaments and FCC Cu channels. A small fraction of HCP phases was also detected, aligning with predictions from the pseudo‐binary phase diagram in Figure 2b, which suggested Ti‐rich HCP precipitates formed during cooling. Minor unindexed peaks, likely attributable to intermetallic phases or oxides formed during the reaction, were observed but had minimal intensity, indicating negligible volume fractions and little impact on composite properties.

The composite structure formed via the LMD process was distributed throughout the material rather than limited to the surface. Figure
5a demonstrates the Cu melt's penetration extended millimeters into the material, underscoring the feasibility of scaling this heat‐conductive composite for larger components. Even at the macroscopic scale, it was clearly observed that Cu selectively replaced only the interdendritic regions while the overall dendritic architecture remained intact. This preservation of structural anisotropy is expected to play a critical role in enhancing the thermal transport properties of the composite. As presented in Figure S4 (Supporting Information), the Cu phase arrangement in the RHEA–Cu composite—fabricated from a dendritic‐structured precursor—was compared to that of a Ta–Cu composite derived from a disordered solid solution precursor. The RHEA–Cu composite exhibited a arrangement‐coherence value of 0.274 (ranging from 0 to 1, with 1 representing perfect alignment), markedly higher than that of the randomly distributed composite (0.054), indicating a significantly greater degree of directional alignment.

caption.p: HEA‐Cu composite with a diffused interface fabricated via the LMD process. a) Overall image of the HEA‐Cu composite captured using OM after the LMD process. b) Nanoindentation measurements of the region, with nano hardness plotted as a function of the distance from the HEA ligament center.

sec.p:
For effective heat conduction, examining the interface between the two phases is critical. Figure
6 presents the microstructure and EDS mapping results analyzed using TEM to closely investigate the interface of the fabricated composite. Consistent with the SEM analysis, the TEM analysis confirms that the interface of this alloy is distinctly separated into RHEA and Cu regions, as shown in Figure 6(a‐1). Figure 6b–e further demonstrate that W, Ta, V, and even Ti primarily reside in the dendritic ligaments of the RHEA.

caption.p: Microstructure of the interface between HEA and Cu channel after the LMD process. a) TEM image of the HEA‐Cu interface and corresponding EDS maps: b) W, c) Ta, d) V, e) Ti. f–k) Mechanism of interface microstructure formation in the HEA‐Cu composite.

sec.p: Notably, TEM analysis identifies two additional microstructural features not observed in the SEM images from Figure 4. The first feature is a W‐rich region. As shown in the figure, the interlayer ≈300 nm thick was observed at all interfaces between the RHEA dendrites and the surrounding Cu. (A more detailed SEM images that we did the TEM‐sampling of the interface has been provided in Figure S5, Supporting Information). As confirmed by TEM‐EDS analysis, this interlayer predominantly comprises W, which correlates with the observed decrease in the average W composition in the dendritic region after the reaction. The second feature is the formation of Ti‐rich precipitates within the HEA interface. This phenomenon is attributed to the recrystallization of Ti, dissolved at the interface during the reaction, into an HCP phase during the cooling process. The XRD trace in Figure 4 also indicates the presence of a small fraction of HCP phases following the LMD process, corroborating the formation of these HCP‐Ti precipitates. These Ti precipitates reduce the amount of Ti dissolved in the dendritic region and proportionally increase the relative concentrations of W and Ta, which are higher‐conductivity elements, potentially enhancing the κ of the composite.

The formation process of this unique structure is illustrated step‐by‐step in the schematic diagram in Figure 6f–k. (For simplicity, the RHEA elements with positive ΔHmix are represented by W, while those exchanged during the process are represented by Ti.) Initially, when the RHEA with a D‐ID structure reacts with the high‐temperature Cu melt, Cu preferentially reacts with the Ti‐rich ID regions (f). Although the Ti in the D regions may also react with Cu, the ID regions contain more than twice as much Ti and exhibit a lower melting point, making it thermodynamically and kinetically more favorable for the reaction to proceed primarily in the ID regions. As a result, the early stage of the reaction predominantly occurs in the ID regions. During this process, Ti, which is miscible with Cu, rapidly exchanges positions at the interface and dissolves into the melt, while Cu atoms occupy the original positions of Ti in the ID regions (g). After sufficient reaction time, all Ti in the ID regions dissolves into the Cu melt, leaving Cu to replace the ID regions. Consequently, the D regions become exposed to the Cu melt (h). With ≈15% Ti still present in the D regions, the remaining Ti also tries to participate in position‐exchange reactions with Cu (i). As a result, the interface near the Cu channel of the RHEA becomes enriched with elements exhibiting positive ΔHmix with Cu. Due to the negligible solubility of these elements in Cu, further position‐exchange reactions cease. Among these, W, which has the highest positive ΔHmix with Cu, remains at the interface, forming a trapped W‐rich interlayer between the two phases (j). During the subsequent cooling process, residual Ti solidifies slowly and recrystallizes behind the W‐rich interlayer into HCP‐phase precipitates (k).

sec.title: Thermal Conductivity of the Fabricated RHEA‐Cu Composite
sec.p:
Figure
7 presents the κ of various alloy materials measured over a range of temperatures. As shown, pure Cu and W exhibit exceptionally high κ at room temperature, ≈398 and 173 W m−1·K−1, respectively. However, consistent with most metals, their κ decreases as temperature increases. Within the temperature range analyzed, pure Cu and W show average declines with slopes of ≈−0.047 and −0.071 W m−1·K− 2, respectively. This reduction is attributed to increased lattice vibrations at higher temperatures, which interfere with the mobility of conduction electrons.

caption.p: Temperature‐dependent thermal conductivity of various alloys. This figure includes the thermal conductivity of pure Cu and W, the WTaVTi alloy, its composite with Cu, as well as previously reported W‐Cu composites.

sec.p: In comparison, W‐Cu composite alloys demonstrate intermediate κ values. For instance, a composite containing ≈25 wt.% Cu exhibits a κ of ≈200 W m−1·K−1 at room temperature. Similar to pure metals, the κ of this composite decreases with temperature at a slope of −0.044 W m−1·K− 2, reaching ≈155 W m−1·K−1 at 1000 °C. This value corresponds to 80% of the κ predicted by the Rule of Mixtures (ROM), highlighting minimal heat loss caused by interfaces or microstructural features. These characteristics qualify the material as an excellent candidate for thermal management applications.

sec.title: Enhancement of Irradiation Resistance of the RHEAs
sec.p:
Fan et al. proposed that the internal pressure (p) within blisters can be used to predict the stress at which cracks form on the blister surface. At ambient temperatures, vacancy diffusion within the blister region is effectively negligible due to the high activation energy required for vacancy migration in W‐based refractory alloys; thus, understanding the internal pressure becomes crucial in evaluating crack initiation. Equation (1) calculates the internal pressure of overpressed bubbles, considering the bubble spacing (d), radius of a bubble (r), surface tension (γ), and average tensile stress (T) across a bubble plane:[
41
]
(1) p=2γr+Td2−πr2r2

To simplify the calculations, several assumptions were made. It was assumed that the WTaVTi alloy has similar r (≈1 nm) and d (≈2 nm) values as W. Although precise values of γ for RHEAs are unattainable, the surface tensions of refractory elements such as W, Ta, V, and Ti have been reported. Using the ROM, which provides accurate γ estimates for high‐alloy binary systems, the γ for WTaVTi was approximated as the average of its constituent elements. The reported γ values for W, Ta, V, and Ti are ≈2.83, 2.68, 2.15, and 1.61 N m−1, respectively, resulting in an estimated γ of ≈2.32 N m−1 for WTaVTi.[
42
–
45a
] The tensile stress (T) was replaced with the compressive YS from Figure 3a, as theoretical YS values are assumed to be equivalent under tensile and compressive stress. For W and WTaVTi, the YS values used were 563 and 1467 MPa, respectively. In Equation (1), the left‐hand term represents the maximum pressure sustainable due to surface tension, while the right‐hand term reflects the material's resistance to cracking based on its strength. Comparing these terms elucidates their respective contributions to blister resistance.

By comparing the left‐hand term (2γr) and right‐hand term (T(d2−πr2)r2), the contribution of each factor can be assessed. The calculated total p for each material are 6.14 and 5.89 GPa, showing a negligible difference of ≈4%. However, for W, which has a relatively high γ, the contributions from the left‐ and right‐hand sides were 5.66 and 0.48 GPa, respectively. In contrast, for the WTaVTi alloy, which exhibits higher material strength, the corresponding values were 4.73 and 1.26 GPa, with the right‐hand value being approximately three times larger than that of W. This comparison highlights that superior irradiation resistance can be achieved by combining high surface energy, as seen in W, with enhancement in strength by alloying. This finding underscores the potential for advancements in material performance not merely by relying on pure W but through the further optimization of RHEA compositions, enabling the development of improved materials for extreme environments.

sec.title: Manipulation of Microstructure in RHEA‐Cu Composite by Process Optimization
sec.p: The compositional changes are evident in the slight reduction in Ti content within the dendrite regions, as shown in Table 1. This suggests that, after the complete reaction between Cu and the ID regions, the Cu melt continued to react with residual Ti in the dendrites over the long reaction period. ≈15% of the Ti, a negative ΔHmix element, remained in the dendrite regions, which could potentially engage in further reactions. Adjusting the reaction temperature or extending the reaction time could enable additional reactions between Cu and the dendrite's residual Ti, allowing for secondary Cu channels within the RHEA ligaments to form.

Therefore, it can be understood that various factors beyond mere thermodynamic relationships influence the kinetics of the LMD reaction. In particular, the melting point (Tm) of a material serves as a critical factor in determining diffusion kinetics and can significantly affect the rate of the LMD process. The Tm of the D and ID regions, calculated via CALPHAD simulations, were ≈2623 and ≈2117 K, respectively. Given the reaction temperature of 1200 °C in the molten Cu bath, these correspond to ≈0.55Tm for the D regions and ≈0.70Tm for the ID regions. For faster reactions, the sacrificial material should ideally have a melting point corresponding to ≈0.7Tm relative to the molten metal bath. For example, lowering the Tm could restrict reactions in the D regions, while adding low‐melting‐point alloying elements or increasing the Cu melt temperature could promote additional reactions in the D regions. These adjustments provide a pathway for tailoring the microstructure and phase distribution within the final RHEA‐Cu composite, enabling process optimization to achieve the desired material properties.

sec.title: Mechanism of the Formation of Self‐Constructed W‐Interlayer
sec.p: The formation of the W‐enriched region also facilitates the precipitation of HCP‐structured Ti‐rich phases. Figure 6k illustrates the final structure of the interface, highlighting these precipitates. Notably, Ti remaining near the W‐interlayer during the cooling process precipitates as an HCP phase, a thermodynamically stable structure for Ti and V at temperatures below 1200 K (as indicated by the blue region in Figure 2b). The EDS maps confirm that these precipitates are Ti‐rich with small amounts of V, consistent with the stable HCP phase at these temperatures. (Figure S6a, Supporting Information shows the binary Ti‐V phase diagram.) The potential locations for these precipitates are conceptually overlaid in Figure 6a, marked by dashed lines. This aligns with observations of conventional Ti alloys, such as Ti‐64, which readily form HCP phases during slow cooling processes like furnace cooling. The over‐saturated Ti at the Cu interface during solidification likely transformed into the HCP phase. Even if the LMD process temperature was as high as 1473 K, the gradual cooling within the furnace would still enable the formation of HCP precipitates in the Ti‐rich interface regions, as supported by the CCT diagram for Ti‐64 alloys shown in Figure S6b (Supporting Information). However, the volume fraction of these precipitates was found to be less than 1 vol.% and was confined to the surface of the RHEA ligaments adjacent to Cu. The Cu channels, which play a dominant role in thermal transport, showed minimal evidence of these precipitates. Therefore, it is expected that their impact on the overall κ of the composite is negligible. This localized formation of HCP phases represents a minor microstructural feature that does not detract from the thermal efficiency of the material.

sec.title: Thermal Conductivity and Interfacial Resistance Analysis of RHEA‐Cu and W‐Cu Composites
sec.p: The κ of the composite is influenced by the κ values of its constituent phases and the energy loss at the interfaces during heat transfer. The RHEA‐Cu composite developed in this study shows relatively low κ at room temperature, as depicted in Figure 7. This suggests that the RHEA‐Cu has significant interfacial energy losses in heat transfer at room temperature. However, the κ increases steeply with temperature (+0.075 W m−1·K− 2 slope) and surpasses that of pure W above 650 °C, indicating a substantial reduction in interfacial energy losses with increasing temperature.

According to DMM, the interfacial thermal efficiency can be quantified using the Diffuse Mismatch Coefficient (DMC), calculated as the ratio of the specific heat (Cp) and sound velocity (v) of the ligament phase to that of the Cu channel as Equation (2) below.
(2) Diffusemismatchcoefficient=(Cp×v)ligament(Cp×v)Cuchannel

Figure
8a illustrates the calculated DMC values for W‐Cu and RHEA‐Cu composites. The input values for Cp​ and v were obtained from the literature, and RHEA ligament (WTaV) properties were estimated using ROM, assuming complete dissolution of Ti into the Cu melt.[
48
–
59a
] (The calculated values for each variable that determines the DMC are detailed by temperature in Figure S7, Supporting Information). At room temperature, the DMC for WTaV‐Cu was ≈0.7, significantly higher than that of W‐Cu (≈0.39). The DMC for WTaV‐Cu increased with temperature, reaching ≈0.84 at 1000 °C, while the W‐Cu DMC remained relatively low (≈0.45). This indicates that heat loss at the RHEA‐Cu interface diminishes with increasing temperature, improving thermal transfer efficiency. In contrast, W‐Cu composites exhibit less temperature‐dependent interfacial resistance, leading to smaller changes in κ.

caption.p: Thermal conductivity and interfacial resistance changes in composite materials based on the DMM model. a) Temperature‐dependent mismatch between WTaV or W and Cu as predicted by the DMM model. b) Normalized thermal conductivity (TC) of HEA‐Cu and W‐Cu composites as a function of Cu fraction, along with the temperature‐dependent thermal conductivity for each fraction.

sec.p: Figure 8b compares the normalized thermal conductivities (κnorm ) of various composites, where κnorm represents the κ normalized by the theoretical maximum (ROM). At room temperature, RHEA‐Cu composites exhibited a low κnorm (≈0.47), dominated by the less conductive RHEA ligament. However, at 800 °C, κnorm increased to ≈0.88, reflecting reduced interfacial losses and enhanced Cu channel contribution. Conversely, κnorm for W‐Cu composites showed minimal change with temperature, consistent with the relatively invariant DMC values.

While DMM cannot fully explain all κ phenomena, the trends observed align well with the diffuse mismatch theory. The RHEA‐Cu composite, which initially showed lower κ than W‐Cu at room temperature, exhibited a dramatic increase with temperature, surpassing W‐Cu composites with similar Cu fractions at ≈500 °C. Additionally, the composite's κ exceeded 120 W m−1·K−1 at 600 °C, outperforming pure W. This temperature range aligns with the operating conditions of molten salt reactors, demonstrating the potential of RHEA‐Cu composites for high‐performance thermal management applications in extreme environments.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p:
This study successfully developed a novel RHEA‐Cu composite using the LMD process, marking a pioneering attempt in material science. The composite exhibits exceptional mechanical properties and κ under high‐temperature conditions, presenting an innovative solution that overcomes the limitations of existing materials. This advancement is highly significant as it marks the development of an exceptional nuclear material that combines remarkable mechanical strength, superior irradiation resistance, and excellent thermal conductivity at elevated temperatures. The primary findings of this research are summarized as follows:
The WTaVTi alloy also exhibited outstanding irradiation resistance, with 30% lower swelling under α‐ion irradiation compared to pure W, a benchmark material for irradiation‐resistant metals. Remarkably, even at ≈57 at.% of He implantation, no swelling or blister‐induced surface cracks were observed, indicating its potential for extensive use in nuclear applications, where materials are exposed to severe irradiation damage.
The composite structure optimized heat conduction pathways through a networked microstructure between the RHEA and Cu phases. Unlike traditional LMD processes, this study employed as‐cast precursors with a highly directional D‐ID structure. This approach deliberately replaced ID regions with Cu to form a directional composite structure, significantly enhancing κ and the bonding performance between plasma‐facing materials (PFM) and water‐cooled Cu pipes.
The LMD process was performed over 96 h at 1200 °C, enabling the reaction in mm‐scale. This achievement contrasts sharply with conventional LMD processes, which are typically limited to surface‐scale reactions. Importantly, the potential of this LMD approach is not limited to a specific system. In particular, HEAs, with their vast compositional diversity, offer far more variation than conventional alloy systems. This opens up opportunities to fabricate entirely new classes of composites or porous materials that were previously unattainable. The success of this long‐duration, large‐volume fabrication represents a critical breakthrough toward industrial‐scale production and commercialization.
The process also led to the spontaneous formation of a unique W‐rich interlayer at the RHEA ligament surface. Unlike commercial W‐Cu materials, which often require additional steps to incorporate interlayers for improved interfacial bonding, the W‐rich interlayer in this study formed autonomously. This feature not only simplifies the process but also ensures excellent interfacial bonding between the two phases, minimizing defects such as voids and reducing κ losses.
While the RHEA‐Cu composite exhibited lower κ at room temperature compared to W‐Cu composites with equivalent Cu fractions, it showed a steep increase with temperature, reaching ≈120 W m−1·K−1 at ≈650 °C, surpassing pure W. This temperature coincides with the operating range of typical molten salt reactors (600–700 °C), highlighting the composite's suitability for nuclear applications. The temperature‐dependent increase in κ can be attributed to the rising DMC between RHEA and Cu, which improved from 0.47 at room temperature to 0.88 at 800 °C, making the composite highly effective at elevated temperatures.

The RHEA‐Cu composite developed in this study represents a groundbreaking advancement in high‐temperature materials, excelling in mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and κ. This composite is poised to become a next‐generation high‐temperature material, with potential applications in nuclear and aerospace industries and beyond. Its unique properties position it as a crucial solution for extreme environments, as well as industries where high‐temperature performance and efficient thermal management are essential.

sec.title: Alloy Fabrications
sec.p: RHEAs, W, WTa, WTaVi, and WTaVTi, were synthesized using an arc‐melter. High‐purity elements (≥99.9%), W, Ta, V, Ti, and Cu were melted under a Ti‐gettered argon atmosphere. To ensure homogeneity, the ingots were melted at least five times, followed by solidification and cooling on a water‐cooled copper (Cu) hearth. The cast alloy ingots were machined into suitable sizes for each experiment using a precision high‐speed saw with a diamond‐metal bonded wafer blade or an electrical discharge machine (EDM). The surfaces of the machined samples were polished with sandpaper up to P2000 grade to minimize the influence of surface roughness during the LMD reaction.

sec.title: Liquid Metal Dealloying (LMD) Process
sec.p: For the LMD process, the precursor alloy (prepared in a coin shape, 1 mm thick, 4 mm diameter, ≈1 g weight) and 100 g of pure Cu (99.999%) were encapsulated in a silica tube under vacuum. The tube was evacuated using a rotary pump. The precursor contained ≈0.1 g of Ti, and any dissolution into the Cu melt was expected to have a negligible effect on Cu purity. To maintain Cu in a liquid state, the tubes were placed in a muffle furnace at 1200 °C for 96 h. After the reaction, the silica tube was quenched in room‐temperature water to cool the material as quickly as possible. Although cracks were observed on the silica tube's surface during cooling, the tube remained robust, preventing direct cooling of the material by the water. Therefore, the precise cooling rate could not be determined. After the reaction, the RHEA‐Cu composite was recovered by grinding away the surrounding Cu parts.

sec.title: Mechanical Testing
sec.p: Compressive tests were conducted on a tensile testing machine (Instron 5967, Instron Inc., USA) at a strain rate of 10⁻3 s⁻¹. The tests covered temperatures ranging from 77 to 1073 K and were terminated when compressive strain exceeded 30%. Rectangular specimens with dimensions of 2 mm × 2 mm × 4 mm were used, and results were averaged over at least three tests.

The nano‐hardness of the materials was measured via nanoindentation (TI 950 Triboindenter, Bruker, USA) using a Berkovich indenter tip. Indentation was performed with a trapezoidal load function, applying a maximum load of 10 mN for 5 s, holding at maximum load for 2 s, and unloading over 5 s. Hardness was calculated from the unloading curve. Indentations were arranged in a 10 × 10 array with a 5 µm spacing between points, resulting in measurements from 100 points, which were plotted as a function of distance from the ligament center.

sec.title: Microstructural Characterization
sec.p: The crystal structure of the specimens was analyzed using an X‐ray diffractometer (D2 Phaser, Bruker) with Cu Kα1 radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm). Scanning was performed at a speed of 15° per min, with an exposure time of 5 s per degree to ensure high‐intensity readings. Microstructural observations were performed using a field‐emission scanning electron microscope (FE‐SEM; Mira3, Tescan, Czech Republic) equipped with an energy‐dispersive spectrometer (EDS; xFlash 6130, Bruker, Germany). Further detailed analysis was conducted using a transmission electron microscope (TEM; JEM‐2100F, JEOL), which was also equipped with an EDS system (Ultim Max TLE, Oxford Instruments, UK) and Aztec TEM EDS software (Oxford Instruments, UK). TEM samples were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB; Helios NanoLab 600, FEI, USA). FIB lamellae were bulk‐out from the interface between the RHEA dendrite and Cu and prepared to a size of ≈10 × 20 µm. These samples were thinned to ≈100 nm and cleaned on both sides at 5 kV for final preparation.

sec.title: Thermal and Electrical Property Measurement
sec.p: Thermal conductivity (κ) was determined by measuring thermal diffusivity (α) using the laser flash method (LFA 457, NETZSCH, Germany) over a temperature range of 298–1173 K in an argon atmosphere. Specific heat (Cp) was measured via differential scanning calorimetry (DSC 8500, PerkinElmer, USA) at a heating rate of 10 K min−1. The density of the alloys was calculated using Archimedes' principle with an electronic balance (XS204, Mettler Toledo, Switzerland). Tridecane was used as a medium for precise measurements due to its higher viscosity and lower density (0.756 g cm− 3) compared to water. The final density values were averaged from five measurements, excluding the maximum and minimum. The resistance of alloy samples (10 × 12 × 0.3 mm) was measured using a physical property measurement system (PPMS‐14, Quantum Design, USA).

sec.title: Ion Implantation and Swelling Measurement
sec.p: The top surface of the disks was mechanically polished to achieve a root‐mean‐square surface roughness of ≈1 nm, verified by atomic force microscopy (AFM) after the final step of mechanical polish (VibroMet, Beuhler, Germany). Helium ion implantation was performed on the polished surface using a focused helium ion beam (ORION Helium Ion Microscope, Zeiss, Germany) at room temperature. Selected areas (10 × 10 µm2) were irradiated with a beam energy of 25 keV and beam currents of 100 pA, resulting in a beam spot size of several nanometers. Irradiation doses ranged from 5 × 10¹⁶ to 1 × 10¹⁸ ions cm− 2, with repeated implantation to reach the desireddoses.
